title: CUET Physics Test 5
subject: Physics (Code: 322)
syllabus_source: CUET SYLLABUS/Physics - 322.pdf (NTA syllabus for CUET (UG) 2026, latest published)
past_paper_reference: Pattern benchmark only: NTA CUET (UG) Physics papers 2024, 2025 and 2026, analysed for format and level (no questions copied)

instructions: Each correct answer earns 5 marks; each incorrect answer deducts 1 mark; unattempted questions earn 0.
Calculators are not allowed; numbers are chosen so the working can be done by hand.

questions.sub_topic: Focal length from a real image three times the object
questions.question: A convex lens forms a real image three times the size of an object placed 20 cm from it. The focal length of the lens is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 15 cm
Given: \(u = -20\) cm, real image, \(m = -3\)
Formula: \(m = \dfrac{v}{u}\), \(\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u}\)
Step 1: \(v = mu = +60\) cm
Step 2: \(\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{60} + \dfrac{1}{20} = \dfrac{4}{60}\), so \(f = 15\) cm
Common mistake: 30 cm (B) uses \(\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u}\) with \(u = -20\) cm.
Key point: A real image from a lens means \(m\) is negative.

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Unit of magnetic susceptibility
questions.question: Magnetic susceptibility \(\chi\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) dimensionless
Why: \(\chi = \dfrac{M}{H}\), and magnetisation \(M\) and intensity \(H\) both have the unit A m⁻¹, so the ratio has no unit.
Why not the others: A m⁻¹ (A) is the unit of \(M\) and \(H\) themselves. Tesla (C) is the unit of \(B\). H m⁻¹ (D) is the unit of permeability.
Key point: \(\mu_r = 1 + \chi\) is also dimensionless.

questions.sub_topic: Average binding energy in the iron-56 nucleus
questions.question: The total binding energy of \(^{56}\text{Fe}\) is about 492 MeV. Its binding energy per nucleon is about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 8.8 MeV
Given: \(E_b = 492\) MeV, \(A = 56\)
Formula: \(\dfrac{E_b}{A}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{492}{56} \approx 8.8\) MeV
Common mistake: 17.6 MeV (D) divides by half the mass number; divide by all 56 nucleons.
Key point: Iron is among the most tightly bound nuclei.

questions.sub_topic: Energy released when two deuterons fuse into helium-4
questions.question: Two deuterons (\(m = 2.014102\) u each) fuse to form a \(^{4}\text{He}\) nucleus (\(m = 4.002603\) u). The energy released is about (1 u = 931.5 MeV):
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 23.8 MeV
Given: reactants \(2 \times 2.014102 = 4.028204\) u; product 4.002603 u
Formula: \(Q = \Delta m \times 931.5\) MeV
Step 1: \(\Delta m = 4.028204 - 4.002603 = 0.025601\) u
Step 2: \(Q = 0.025601 \times 931.5 \approx 23.8\) MeV
Common mistake: 11.9 MeV (B) halves the result, as if giving the energy per deuteron.
Key point: Fusion of light nuclei releases energy because the product is more tightly bound.

questions.sub_topic: Electric field amplitude from B₀ = 2 × 10⁻⁸ T
questions.question: The magnetic field amplitude of an EM wave in vacuum is \(2 \times 10^{-8}\) T. Its electric field amplitude is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 6 V m⁻¹
Given: \(B_0 = 2 \times 10^{-8}\) T
Formula: \(E_0 = cB_0\)
Step 1: \(E_0 = 3 \times 10^8 \times 2 \times 10^{-8} = 6\) V m⁻¹
Common mistake: \(6.7 \times 10^{-17}\) (B) divides by \(c\).
Key point: \(\dfrac{E_0}{B_0} = c\).

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Point of zero field between two parallel currents
questions.question: Two long parallel wires 8 cm apart carry 2 A and 6 A in the same direction. The magnetic field is zero at a point between them at a distance of:
options: A) 6 cm from the 2 A wire
C) 2 cm from the 6 A wire
D) 2 cm from the 2 A wire
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 2 cm from the 2 A wire
Given: \(I_1 = 2\) A, \(I_2 = 6\) A, separation 8 cm; let the point be \(x\) from the 2 A wire
Formula: \(\dfrac{\mu_0I_1}{2\pi x} = \dfrac{\mu_0I_2}{2\pi(8 - x)}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{2}{x} = \dfrac{6}{8 - x} \Rightarrow 16 - 2x = 6x\)
Step 2: \(x = 2\) cm from the 2 A wire
Common mistake: (C) puts the point near the larger current; it must be nearer the smaller one to balance.
Key point: For like currents the zero-field point lies between the wires, nearer the weaker current.

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Fields, energy and torque of a bar magnet
questions.question:
Match each quantity for a short bar magnet of moment \(m\) in List-I with its expression in List-II.

List-I
(A) Field at a distant axial point
(B) Field at a distant equatorial point
(C) Potential energy in a uniform field \(B\)
(D) Torque in a uniform field \(B\)

List-II
(I) \(\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{m}{r^3}\)
(II) \(mB\sin\theta\)
(III) \(\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{r^3}\)
(IV) \(-mB\cos\theta\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Step 1: Axial field: \(\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{r^3}\) (III)
Step 2: Equatorial field: half the axial value (I)
Step 3: Potential energy: \(-mB\cos\theta\) (IV)
Step 4: Torque: \(mB\sin\theta\) (II)
Common mistake: Swapping (C) and (D); energy uses cosine (least at \(\theta = 0\)), torque uses sine (zero at \(\theta = 0\)).
Key point: A bar magnet's field has the same form as an electric dipole's.

questions.sub_topic: Dipole moment of a pair of charges
questions.question: Charges of \(+5\) nC and \(-5\) nC are 4 mm apart. The electric dipole moment of this pair is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(2 \times 10^{-11}\) C m
Given: \(q = 5 \times 10^{-9}\) C, \(2a = 4 \times 10^{-3}\) m
Formula: \(p = q \times 2a\)
Step 1: \(p = 5 \times 10^{-9} \times 4 \times 10^{-3} = 2 \times 10^{-11}\) C m
Common mistake: \(1 \times 10^{-11}\) (A) uses half the separation.
Key point: The dipole moment points from the negative to the positive charge.

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Magnetic moment from the maximum torque on a coil
questions.question: The greatest torque on a current loop in a uniform field of 0.1 T is 0.02 N m. The magnetic moment of the loop is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 0.2 A m²
Given: \(\tau_{max} = 0.02\) N m, \(B = 0.1\) T
Formula: \(\tau_{max} = mB\)
Step 1: \(m = \dfrac{0.02}{0.1} = 0.2\) A m²
Common mistake: 0.002 A m² (B) multiplies \(\tau\) by \(B\). 5 A m² (C) inverts the ratio.
Key point: The torque is greatest when the moment is perpendicular to \(B\).

questions.sub_topic: Four a.c. circuits in increasing order of impedance
questions.question:
Arrange these series circuits (at the supply frequency) in increasing order of impedance:
(A) \(R = 30\ \Omega\) only
(B) \(R = 30\ \Omega\), \(X_L = 40\ \Omega\)
(C) \(R = 20\ \Omega\), \(X_L = X_C = 100\ \Omega\)
(D) \(R = 60\ \Omega\), \(X_L = 80\ \Omega\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C), (A), (B), (D)
Step 1: (A) \(Z = 30\ \Omega\); (B) \(\sqrt{900 + 1600} = 50\ \Omega\)
Step 2: (C) resonance: \(Z = R = 20\ \Omega\); (D) \(\sqrt{3600 + 6400} = 100\ \Omega\)
Step 3: Increasing: (C), (A), (B), (D)
Common mistake: Adding all the reactances in (C) and placing it last; \(X_L\) and \(X_C\) cancel.
Key point: \(Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}\).

questions.sub_topic: Number of spectral lines from the n = 4 level
questions.question: Hydrogen atoms are excited to the \(n = 4\) level. The number of different spectral lines they can emit in returning to the ground state is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 6
Given: highest level \(n = 4\)
Formula: number of lines \(= \dfrac{n(n - 1)}{2}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{4 \times 3}{2} = 6\)
Step 2: They are 4→3, 4→2, 4→1, 3→2, 3→1, 2→1
Common mistake: 3 (C) counts only the jumps from \(n = 4\).
Key point: Every pair of levels gives one line.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.sub_topic: How photoelectric quantities depend on intensity, frequency and momentum
questions.question:
Match each relation in List-I with its behaviour in List-II.

List-I
(A) Photocurrent versus intensity (fixed frequency above threshold)
(B) Maximum kinetic energy versus frequency
(C) Stopping potential versus intensity
(D) de Broglie wavelength versus momentum

List-II
(I) Independent
(II) Increases linearly above the threshold frequency
(III) Directly proportional
(IV) Inversely proportional
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(III), (B)-(II), (C)-(I), (D)-(IV)
Step 1: More photons, more electrons: photocurrent \(\propto\) intensity (III)
Step 2: \(K_{max} = h\nu - \phi_0\): a straight line starting at \(\nu_0\) (II)
Step 3: \(V_0\) depends on \(\nu\), not on intensity (I)
Step 4: \(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p}\) (IV)
Common mistake: Swapping (A) and (C); intensity changes the current, not the stopping potential.
Key point: The wave picture wrongly predicted that intensity would raise the electrons' energy.

questions.sub_topic: Equivalent resistance of a four-resistor network
questions.question: Two \(4\ \Omega\) resistors in parallel are joined in series with an \(8\ \Omega\) resistor, and this whole combination is connected in parallel with a \(10\ \Omega\) resistor. The equivalent resistance is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(5\ \Omega\)
Step 1: \(4 \parallel 4 = 2\ \Omega\)
Step 2: \(2 + 8 = 10\ \Omega\)
Step 3: \(10 \parallel 10 = 5\ \Omega\)
Common mistake: \(26\ \Omega\) (C) adds every resistor in series.
Key point: Two equal resistors in parallel give half of one.

questions.sub_topic: Current through an inductor of 1/π H on the mains
questions.question: A pure inductor of \(\dfrac{1}{\pi}\) H is connected to a 220 V, 50 Hz supply. The rms current is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 2.2 A
Given: \(L = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\) H, \(\nu = 50\) Hz, \(V = 220\) V
Formula: \(X_L = 2\pi\nu L\), \(I = \dfrac{V}{X_L}\)
Step 1: \(X_L = 2\pi \times 50 \times \dfrac{1}{\pi} = 100\ \Omega\)
Step 2: \(I = \dfrac{220}{100} = 2.2\) A
Common mistake: 0.7 A (B) uses \(X_L \approx 314\ \Omega\), forgetting that the \(\pi\) cancels.
Key point: The \(\pi\) in such values is chosen to cancel the \(2\pi\nu\).

questions.sub_topic: Units of induction and a.c. quantities
questions.question:
Match each quantity in List-I with its SI unit in List-II.

List-I
(A) Magnetic flux
(B) Inductance
(C) Reactance
(D) Rate of change of magnetic flux

List-II
(I) volt
(II) ohm
(III) henry
(IV) weber
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Step 1: Flux: weber (IV)
Step 2: Inductance: henry (III)
Step 3: Reactance, like resistance: ohm (II)
Step 4: \(\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}\) is an emf: Wb s⁻¹ = volt (I)
Common mistake: Swapping (A) and (B); henry = weber per ampere.
Key point: 1 V = 1 Wb s⁻¹.

questions.sub_topic: Resistance ratio of two wires of different length and diameter
questions.question: Two wires of the same material have lengths in the ratio 1 : 2 and diameters in the ratio 2 : 1. The ratio of their resistances is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1 : 8
Given: \(\dfrac{l_1}{l_2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), \(\dfrac{d_1}{d_2} = 2\)
Formula: \(R = \dfrac{\rho l}{A} \propto \dfrac{l}{d^2}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{R_1}{R_2} = \dfrac{l_1}{l_2} \times \left(\dfrac{d_2}{d_1}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{4}\)
Step 2: \(= \dfrac{1}{8}\)
Common mistake: 1 : 2 (A) uses the diameter instead of its square.
Key point: Area goes as diameter squared.

questions.sub_topic: How the electron's orbital speed changes with n
questions.question: In the Bohr model of hydrogen, as the principal quantum number \(n\) increases, the speed of the electron in its orbit:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) decreases
Why: \(v_n = \dfrac{e^2}{2\varepsilon_0nh}\), so \(v \propto \dfrac{1}{n}\); outer orbits are slower.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) contradict \(v \propto \dfrac{1}{n}\).
Key point: In the ground state \(v \approx 2.2 \times 10^6\) m s⁻¹, about \(\dfrac{c}{137}\).

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.sub_topic: Stopping potential when the wavelength is halved
questions.question: Light of wavelength 413 nm ejects photoelectrons from a metal of work function 2 eV. If the wavelength is halved, the new stopping potential is about (\(hc = 1240\) eV nm):
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 4 V
Given: \(\lambda_1 = 413\) nm, \(\phi_0 = 2\) eV, \(\lambda_2 = 206.5\) nm
Formula: \(eV_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - \phi_0\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{1240}{413} \approx 3\) eV, so the photon energy at \(\dfrac{\lambda}{2}\) is 6 eV
Step 2: \(eV_0 = 6 - 2 = 4\) eV, so \(V_0 = 4\) V
Common mistake: 2 V (A) doubles the old stopping potential (1 V); halving \(\lambda\) doubles the photon energy, not \(K_{max}\).
Key point: The work function is subtracted after the photon energy changes.

questions.sub_topic: What Young's double-slit experiment demonstrates
questions.question: Young's double-slit experiment directly demonstrates:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) interference
Why: Light from two coherent slits overlaps and forms bright and dark fringes where the waves add or cancel.
Why not the others: Reflection and refraction (A, B) are explained by rays as well as waves. Dispersion (D) needs a medium whose index varies with wavelength.
Key point: Fringes are the signature of the wave nature of light.

questions.sub_topic: Series LCR resonance and reactance — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) At resonance, the impedance of a series LCR circuit is a minimum.
(B) The power factor of a purely resistive circuit is 1.
(C) At resonance, the current in a series LCR circuit is in phase with the applied voltage.
(D) Inductive reactance decreases as the frequency increases.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) \(X_L = X_C\), so \(Z = R\). (B) \(\phi = 0\), \(\cos\phi = 1\). (C) the reactances cancel, leaving a resistive circuit.
Why not the others: (D) is false: \(X_L = \omega L\) rises with frequency. Options (C) and (D) include (D); (B) leaves out (C).
Key point: Resonance makes a series LCR circuit behave like a pure resistor.

questions.sub_topic: Origin and nature of EM waves — which claims fail
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Displacement current arises from a changing electric field.
(B) A charge oscillating at frequency \(\nu\) radiates EM waves of frequency \(\nu\).
(C) A charge moving with constant velocity radiates EM waves.
(D) There are no sharp boundaries between neighbouring bands of the EM spectrum.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C) only
Why: Only (C) is false: only accelerated charges radiate; a steadily moving charge has fields that move with it.
Why not the others: (A) \(i_d = \varepsilon_0\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt}\). (B) the radiated wave has the source's frequency. (D) the bands overlap and are named by how they are produced or detected. Options (A), (B) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Acceleration of charge is the source of all EM radiation.

questions.sub_topic: Potential difference along a line at 60° to a uniform field
questions.question: In a uniform electric field of 200 V m⁻¹, two points are 5 cm apart on a line making \(60^\circ\) with the field. The potential difference between them is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 5 V
Given: \(E = 200\) V m⁻¹, \(d = 0.05\) m, \(\theta = 60^\circ\)
Formula: \(\Delta V = Ed\cos\theta\)
Step 1: Separation along the field \(= 0.05 \times 0.5 = 0.025\) m
Step 2: \(\Delta V = 200 \times 0.025 = 5\) V
Common mistake: 10 V (A) takes the full 5 cm along the field. 8.7 V (B) uses \(\sin 60^\circ\).
Key point: Only the displacement along the field changes the potential.

questions.sub_topic: Terminal voltage of a battery being charged
questions.question: An 8 V battery of internal resistance \(0.5\ \Omega\) is charged from a 120 V d.c. supply through a series resistor of \(15.5\ \Omega\). The terminal voltage of the battery during charging is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 11.5 V
Given: supply 120 V, \(\varepsilon = 8\) V opposing, \(R = 15.5\ \Omega\), \(r = 0.5\ \Omega\)
Formula: \(I = \dfrac{120 - 8}{R + r}\); charging: \(V = \varepsilon + Ir\)
Step 1: \(I = \dfrac{112}{16} = 7\) A
Step 2: \(V = 8 + 7 \times 0.5 = 11.5\) V
Common mistake: 4.5 V (C) uses \(V = \varepsilon - Ir\), the discharging formula.
Key point: While charging, current enters at the positive terminal, so \(V > \varepsilon\).

questions.sub_topic: Angle of refraction for 60° incidence on glass of index √3
questions.question: Light falls on a glass surface (\(n = \sqrt{3}\)) at an angle of incidence of \(60^\circ\). The angle of refraction is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(30^\circ\)
Given: \(i = 60^\circ\), \(n = \sqrt{3}\)
Formula: \(\sin i = n\sin r\)
Step 1: \(\sin r = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}/2}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)
Step 2: \(r = 30^\circ\)
Common mistake: \(60^\circ\) (A) assumes the ray goes straight on.
Key point: Light entering a denser medium bends towards the normal.

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Current needed for a given solenoid field
questions.question: A long solenoid has 2000 turns per metre. The current needed to produce a field of 0.01 T inside it is about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 4 A
Given: \(n = 2000\) m⁻¹, \(B = 0.01\) T
Formula: \(I = \dfrac{B}{\mu_0n}\)
Step 1: \(\mu_0n = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 2000 \approx 2.5 \times 10^{-3}\)
Step 2: \(I = \dfrac{0.01}{2.5 \times 10^{-3}} = 4\) A
Common mistake: 0.4 A (B) or 40 A (C) slips a power of ten in \(\mu_0n\).
Key point: The field inside a solenoid depends on turns per metre, not on its radius.

questions.sub_topic: Band with the longest wavelength
questions.question: Which of these has the longest wavelength?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) radio waves
Why: Radio waves have wavelengths from about 0.1 m to many kilometres, longer than any other band.
Why not the others: Infrared is around micrometres, ultraviolet around 10–400 nm, gamma rays below \(10^{-3}\) nm.
Key point: Order of wavelength: radio > micro > IR > visible > UV > X > gamma.

questions.sub_topic: Current and drift — which claims fail
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Free electrons in a conductor drift opposite to the applied electric field.
(B) The drift speed of electrons in a wire is typically about a millimetre per second or less.
(C) Electric current is a vector quantity.
(D) The resistivity of alloys such as manganin changes very little with temperature.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C) only
Why: Only (C) is false: current has a direction along the wire but does not add by the vector law at a junction, so it is a scalar.
Why not the others: (A) electrons are negative. (B) \(v_d\) is small even for large currents. (D) this is why manganin is used for standard resistors. Options (A), (B) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Current density is a vector; current is a scalar.

questions.sub_topic: Size of the image of a 5 cm object in a concave mirror
questions.question: A 5 cm tall object stands 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. The image is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 2.5 cm tall, inverted
Given: \(u = -30\) cm, \(f = -10\) cm, \(h_o = 5\) cm
Formula: \(\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}\), \(m = -\dfrac{v}{u}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{1}{v} = -\dfrac{1}{10} + \dfrac{1}{30} = -\dfrac{1}{15}\), so \(v = -15\) cm
Step 2: \(m = -\dfrac{-15}{-30} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\); \(h_i = -2.5\) cm (inverted)
Common mistake: (C) gets the size but drops the sign; a real image from a mirror is inverted.
Key point: Negative magnification means an inverted image.

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Force on a wire perpendicular to a field
questions.question: A wire 20 cm long carrying 3 A is placed perpendicular to a uniform field of 0.5 T. The force on it is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 0.3 N
Given: \(I = 3\) A, \(l = 0.2\) m, \(B = 0.5\) T
Formula: \(F = IlB\)
Step 1: \(F = 3 \times 0.2 \times 0.5 = 0.3\) N
Common mistake: 3 N (A) uses 20 cm as 2 m.
Key point: The force is greatest when the wire is perpendicular to the field.

questions.sub_topic: Charge found from field and potential at a point
questions.question: At a point near an isolated point charge, the field is 500 N C⁻¹ and the potential is 3000 V. The charge is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(2\ \mu\text{C}\)
Given: \(E = 500\) N C⁻¹, \(V = 3000\) V
Formula: \(V = \dfrac{kq}{r}\), \(E = \dfrac{kq}{r^2}\), so \(r = \dfrac{V}{E}\)
Step 1: \(r = \dfrac{3000}{500} = 6\) m
Step 2: \(q = \dfrac{Vr}{k} = \dfrac{3000 \times 6}{9 \times 10^9} = 2 \times 10^{-6}\) C
Common mistake: \(0.33\ \mu\text{C}\) (B) takes \(r = 1\) m instead of finding it from \(\dfrac{V}{E}\).
Key point: For a point charge, \(\dfrac{V}{E}\) equals the distance.

questions.sub_topic: Force on a charge near a large charged sheet
questions.question: A large thin sheet carries a uniform charge density of \(8.85 \times 10^{-8}\) C m⁻². The force on a charge of \(2\ \mu\text{C}\) near it is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 0.01 N
Given: \(\sigma = 8.85 \times 10^{-8}\) C m⁻², \(q = 2 \times 10^{-6}\) C
Formula: \(E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\), \(F = qE\)
Step 1: \(E = \dfrac{8.85 \times 10^{-8}}{2 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12}} = 5000\) N C⁻¹
Step 2: \(F = 2 \times 10^{-6} \times 5000 = 0.01\) N
Common mistake: 0.02 N (A) uses \(\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\), the field near a conductor.
Key point: The field of a large sheet does not depend on distance.

questions.sub_topic: Fission and fusion — which claims fail
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) In nuclear fission, a heavy nucleus splits into two lighter nuclei.
(B) Nuclear fusion needs very high temperatures.
(C) The energy of the Sun comes mainly from nuclear fusion.
(D) In both fission and fusion, the total mass of the products is greater than that of the reactants.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (D) only
Why: Only (D) is false: in both processes the products are lighter; the lost mass appears as energy, \(E = \Delta mc^2\).
Why not the others: (A) e.g. \(^{235}\text{U}\) splits into barium and krypton. (B) nuclei must overcome their Coulomb repulsion. (C) the Sun fuses hydrogen into helium. Options (A), (B) and (C) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Both processes move nuclei towards the peak of the binding energy curve.

questions.sub_topic: What acceptor atoms become after taking electrons
questions.question: In a p-type semiconductor, an acceptor atom that has accepted an electron becomes:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) a negative ion
Why: The trivalent atom gains an extra electron from a neighbouring bond, so it carries a net negative charge, fixed in the lattice; the hole left behind moves.
Why not the others: (A) it has one electron too many. (B) the hole is in the neighbouring bond, not the atom. (C) positive ions are formed by donors.
Key point: Fixed negative acceptor ions balance the mobile holes, keeping p-type neutral.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.sub_topic: Photons of four radiations in increasing order of momentum
questions.question:
Arrange photons of these radiations in increasing order of momentum:
(A) red light, 700 nm
(B) X-ray, 1 nm
(C) microwave, 1 cm
(D) ultraviolet, 100 nm
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (C), (A), (D), (B)
Step 1: \(p = \dfrac{h}{\lambda}\), so momentum rises as wavelength falls
Step 2: Wavelength: 1 cm > 700 nm > 100 nm > 1 nm
Step 3: Increasing momentum: (C), (A), (D), (B)
Common mistake: (A) lists the photons in decreasing momentum.
Key point: Short-wavelength photons carry the most momentum and energy.

questions.sub_topic: SI units of electrostatic quantities
questions.question:
Match each quantity in List-I with its SI unit in List-II.

List-I
(A) Electric flux
(B) Permittivity of free space \(\varepsilon_0\)
(C) Electric field
(D) Surface charge density

List-II
(I) V m⁻¹
(II) N m² C⁻¹
(III) C m⁻²
(IV) C² N⁻¹ m⁻²
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Step 1: \(\Phi = EA\): (N C⁻¹)(m²) = N m² C⁻¹ (II)
Step 2: From \(F = \dfrac{q_1q_2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2}\): \(\varepsilon_0\) in C² N⁻¹ m⁻² (IV)
Step 3: \(E = \dfrac{V}{d}\): V m⁻¹, the same as N C⁻¹ (I)
Step 4: \(\sigma = \dfrac{q}{A}\): C m⁻² (III)
Common mistake: Swapping (A) and (B); flux has C in the denominator, \(\varepsilon_0\) has C² in the numerator.
Key point: V m⁻¹ and N C⁻¹ are the same unit.

questions.sub_topic: Number of fringes when the wavelength changes
questions.question: In Young's experiment, 10 bright fringes fill a certain width of the screen with light of 600 nm. With light of 400 nm, the number of fringes in the same width is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 15
Given: \(N_1 = 10\), \(\lambda_1 = 600\) nm, \(\lambda_2 = 400\) nm
Formula: \(N\beta\) = fixed width; \(\beta \propto \lambda\), so \(N \propto \dfrac{1}{\lambda}\)
Step 1: \(N_2 = 10 \times \dfrac{600}{400} = 15\)
Common mistake: 6.7 (C) multiplies by \(\dfrac{400}{600}\), assuming more fringes with longer wavelength.
Key point: Shorter wavelength gives narrower fringes, so more fit in.

questions.sub_topic: Capacitors in increasing order of stored energy
questions.question:
Arrange these charged capacitors in increasing order of the energy stored:
(A) \(2\ \mu\text{F}\) at 10 V
(B) \(1\ \mu\text{F}\) at 20 V
(C) \(4\ \mu\text{F}\) at 5 V
(D) \(0.5\ \mu\text{F}\) at 30 V
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (C), (A), (B), (D)
Step 1: \(U = \dfrac{1}{2}CV^2\)
Step 2: (A) \(100\ \mu\text{J}\); (B) \(200\ \mu\text{J}\); (C) \(50\ \mu\text{J}\); (D) \(225\ \mu\text{J}\)
Step 3: Increasing: (C), (A), (B), (D)
Common mistake: Ordering by \(C\) alone; the voltage enters squared, so it matters more.
Key point: Doubling \(V\) stores four times the energy.

questions.sub_topic: Terminal voltage of a battery delivering current
questions.question: A 12 V battery of internal resistance \(0.5\ \Omega\) delivers a current of 4 A. Its terminal voltage is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 10 V
Given: \(\varepsilon = 12\) V, \(r = 0.5\ \Omega\), \(I = 4\) A
Formula: \(V = \varepsilon - Ir\)
Step 1: \(Ir = 2\) V
Step 2: \(V = 12 - 2 = 10\) V
Common mistake: 14 V (A) adds \(Ir\), which applies only while the battery is being charged.
Key point: A discharging cell's terminal voltage is below its emf.

questions.sub_topic: Angular width of a fringe in Young's experiment
questions.question: In Young's experiment the slits are 0.2 mm apart and the light has a wavelength of 600 nm. The angular width of a fringe is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(3 \times 10^{-3}\) rad
Given: \(\lambda = 6 \times 10^{-7}\) m, \(d = 2 \times 10^{-4}\) m
Formula: \(\theta = \dfrac{\lambda}{d}\)
Step 1: \(\theta = \dfrac{6 \times 10^{-7}}{2 \times 10^{-4}} = 3 \times 10^{-3}\) rad
Common mistake: \(6 \times 10^{-3}\) (C) uses \(\dfrac{2\lambda}{d}\), the single-slit central width formula.
Key point: The angular fringe width does not depend on the screen distance.

questions.sub_topic: Magnifying power and power formulas
questions.question:
Match each quantity in List-I with its expression in List-II (\(D\) = least distance of distinct vision, \(L\) = tube length).

List-I
(A) Magnifying power of a simple microscope (image at infinity)
(B) Magnifying power of a compound microscope (image at infinity)
(C) Magnifying power of a telescope in normal adjustment
(D) Power of a lens

List-II
(I) \(\dfrac{D}{f}\)
(II) \(\dfrac{1}{f}\)
(III) \(\dfrac{f_o}{f_e}\)
(IV) \(\dfrac{L}{f_o}\cdot\dfrac{D}{f_e}\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(I), (B)-(IV), (C)-(III), (D)-(II)
Step 1: Simple microscope: \(\dfrac{D}{f}\) (I)
Step 2: Compound: objective \(\dfrac{L}{f_o}\) times eyepiece \(\dfrac{D}{f_e}\) (IV)
Step 3: Telescope: \(\dfrac{f_o}{f_e}\) (III)
Step 4: Power: \(\dfrac{1}{f}\) (II)
Common mistake: Swapping (A) and (B); the compound microscope has two lenses, so two factors.
Key point: A telescope needs a long \(f_o\); a microscope needs short focal lengths.

questions.sub_topic: Rectifiers and ideal diodes
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Half-wave rectifier
(B) Full-wave rectifier (centre-tap)
(C) Ideal diode, forward biased
(D) Ideal diode, reverse biased

List-II
(I) Acts as an open switch
(II) Uses one diode; output in alternate half-cycles
(III) Uses two diodes; output in both half-cycles
(IV) Acts as a closed switch
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(I)
Step 1: Half-wave: one diode conducts in one half-cycle only (II)
Step 2: Centre-tap full-wave: two diodes conduct in turn (III)
Step 3: Forward-biased ideal diode: zero resistance, a closed switch (IV)
Step 4: Reverse-biased ideal diode: infinite resistance, an open switch (I)
Common mistake: Swapping (C) and (D); forward bias lets current through.
Key point: An ideal diode is a one-way switch.

questions.sub_topic: Power in one of two resistors in parallel
questions.question: Resistors of \(6\ \Omega\) and \(3\ \Omega\) are connected in parallel across a 6 V source of negligible internal resistance. The power dissipated in the \(3\ \Omega\) resistor is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 12 W
Given: \(V = 6\) V across each resistor
Formula: \(P = \dfrac{V^2}{R}\)
Step 1: \(P_3 = \dfrac{36}{3} = 12\) W
Common mistake: 18 W (B) is the total power in both resistors. 6 W (A) is the power in the \(6\ \Omega\) resistor.
Key point: In parallel, the smaller resistance takes more power.

questions.sub_topic: Minimum deviation for a 60° prism of index √3
questions.question: A prism of angle \(60^\circ\) is made of glass of refractive index \(\sqrt{3}\). Its angle of minimum deviation is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(60^\circ\)
Given: \(A = 60^\circ\), \(n = \sqrt{3}\)
Formula: \(n = \dfrac{\sin\frac{A + \delta_m}{2}}{\sin\frac{A}{2}}\)
Step 1: \(\sin\dfrac{A + \delta_m}{2} = \sqrt{3} \times \sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{60^\circ + \delta_m}{2} = 60^\circ\), so \(\delta_m = 60^\circ\)
Common mistake: \(30^\circ\) (A) uses the thin-prism formula \((n - 1)A\) with \(n \approx 1.5\), which does not hold for a \(60^\circ\) prism.
Key point: At minimum deviation, \(r = \dfrac{A}{2}\).

questions.sub_topic: Donor density from one part per million of arsenic
questions.question: Silicon has about \(5 \times 10^{28}\) atoms per m³. It is doped with arsenic at one part per million. The number of donor atoms per m³ is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(5 \times 10^{22}\)
Given: \(N_{Si} = 5 \times 10^{28}\) m⁻³, ratio \(10^{-6}\)
Formula: \(N_D = N_{Si} \times 10^{-6}\)
Step 1: \(N_D = 5 \times 10^{22}\) m⁻³
Common mistake: \(5 \times 10^{34}\) (A) multiplies by \(10^6\) instead of dividing.
Key point: Even one part per million gives far more donors than the intrinsic carrier density (about \(10^{16}\) m⁻³).

questions.sub_topic: Radius of the circle of light above a source under water
questions.question: A small bulb lies \(\sqrt{7}\) m below the surface of water (\(n = \dfrac{4}{3}\)). Light leaves the surface only through a circle directly above the bulb. The radius of this circle is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 3 m
Given: \(h = \sqrt{7}\) m, \(\sin C = \dfrac{1}{n} = \dfrac{3}{4}\)
Formula: \(r = h\tan C\)
Step 1: \(\cos C = \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{9}{16}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{7}}{4}\), so \(\tan C = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{7}}\)
Step 2: \(r = \sqrt{7} \times \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{7}} = 3\) m
Common mistake: \(\sqrt{7}\) m (A) takes the critical angle as \(45^\circ\).
Key point: Rays beyond the critical angle are totally reflected back into the water.

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Kinetic energy of a proton on a 10 cm circle
questions.question: A proton moves in a circle of radius 10 cm in a uniform field of 0.5 T. Its kinetic energy is about (\(m_p = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\) kg):
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 0.12 MeV
Given: \(r = 0.1\) m, \(B = 0.5\) T, \(q = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C
Formula: \(r = \dfrac{mv}{qB} \Rightarrow K = \dfrac{q^2B^2r^2}{2m}\)
Step 1: \(q^2B^2r^2 = 2.56 \times 10^{-38} \times 0.25 \times 0.01 = 6.4 \times 10^{-41}\)
Step 2: \(K = \dfrac{6.4 \times 10^{-41}}{3.34 \times 10^{-27}} \approx 1.9 \times 10^{-14}\) J \(\approx 0.12\) MeV
Common mistake: 0.24 MeV (A) forgets the \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) in \(\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2\).
Key point: 1 MeV = \(1.6 \times 10^{-13}\) J.

questions.sub_topic: Average power in a resistor from the peak voltage
questions.question: An a.c. voltage of peak value 100 V is applied across a \(10\ \Omega\) resistor. The average power dissipated is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 500 W
Given: \(V_0 = 100\) V, \(R = 10\ \Omega\)
Formula: \(P = \dfrac{V_{rms}^2}{R}\), \(V_{rms}^2 = \dfrac{V_0^2}{2}\)
Step 1: \(V_{rms}^2 = 5000\)
Step 2: \(P = \dfrac{5000}{10} = 500\) W
Common mistake: 1000 W (A) uses the peak voltage in \(\dfrac{V^2}{R}\).
Key point: Average a.c. power uses rms values.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.sub_topic: Threshold, work function and number of photoelectrons — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Photoelectric emission occurs only if the frequency of light is at least the threshold frequency.
(B) The work function differs from one metal to another.
(C) Alkali metals such as caesium show photoemission with visible light.
(D) Raising the frequency of light at fixed intensity increases the number of photoelectrons emitted per second.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) below \(\nu_0\) no electrons come out, however intense the light. (B) \(\phi_0\) depends on the metal and its surface. (C) caesium's work function is about 2 eV, within visible photon energies.
Why not the others: (D) is false: the number of electrons depends on the number of photons; at fixed intensity, higher frequency means fewer, more energetic photons. Options (C) and (D) include (D); (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: Frequency sets each electron's energy; intensity sets how many.

questions.sub_topic: Charge driven round a coil by a change of flux
questions.question: A coil of 20 turns and resistance \(10\ \Omega\) is in a magnetic field. The flux through each turn falls from 0.5 Wb to zero in 0.1 s. The charge that flows through the coil is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1 C
Given: \(N = 20\), \(\Delta\Phi = 0.5\) Wb, \(R = 10\ \Omega\), \(\Delta t = 0.1\) s
Formula: \(Q = I\Delta t = \dfrac{N\Delta\Phi}{R}\)
Step 1: emf \(= \dfrac{20 \times 0.5}{0.1} = 100\) V; \(I = 10\) A
Step 2: \(Q = 10 \times 0.1 = 1\) C (equivalently \(\dfrac{20 \times 0.5}{10}\))
Common mistake: 10 C (A) is the current in amperes, not the charge.
Key point: The charge depends only on the change of flux, not on how fast it happens.

questions.sub_topic: Properties of electric field lines — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about electric field lines:
(A) They start on positive charges and end on negative charges.
(B) Two field lines never cross each other.
(C) Where the lines are closer together, the field is stronger.
(D) A field line is always the path followed by a free positive charge released on it.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) that is the convention for drawing them. (B) at a crossing the field would have two directions. (C) line density represents field strength.
Why not the others: (D) is false: a field line gives the direction of force, i.e. of acceleration, not of velocity; a charge follows a curved line only in special cases. Options (B) and (D) include (D); (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: A tangent to a field line gives the direction of the field there.
